studies.title: What 141,000 Consumer Complaints Reveal About Why Disputes Escalate in Poorer Neighborhoods
studies.paper_title: Perceived-Control Salience in Service Recovery: Area-Level Economic Disadvantage and Consumer Disputes
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed 141,251 complaint narratives filed with the U.S. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, coding each for seven kinds of "perceived control" language and linking them to whether the consumer escalated into a formal dispute. In economically disadvantaged areas, cues tied to cognitive control (understanding what is happening) and behavioral control (being able to act) were most strongly associated with escalation, while information-control cues — simple disclosure — were associated with *less* escalation.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that in financial services, disputes are driven less by the failure itself than by whether people can comprehend and act on the remedy, and that firms leaning on disclosure as their recovery tool may be addressing the wrong problem.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audit your recovery flows for comprehension burden and action cost — how many steps, forms and reading-level hurdles separate a complaint from a resolution — and test whether simplifying them reduces escalation, rather than assuming more disclosure counts as support.
studies.story_angle_secondary: When a bank or lender messes up, the thing that most predicts whether a complaint turns into a fight is not the money at stake but whether the customer can figure out what happened and do something about it — which is exactly where low-income consumers are most often left stranded.
studies.caveats: Observational analysis of self-selected complaint narratives from a single U.S. regulator and sector (consumer finance); associations, not causal effects; area-level economic disadvantage is a proxy for individual circumstances.
studies.verdict_notes: Study facts and the direction of all reported associations match the abstract; the "Why it matters" line implies a comparison with failure severity that the abstract never tests.

studies.title: When Rival Airlines Share the Same Big Investors, Service Gets Worse and Fares Go Up
studies.journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
studies.the_study: Using a multi-market dataset of U.S. airlines spanning 1995 to 2025, researchers examined whether "common ownership" — rival carriers holding overlapping institutional investors — shows up in the marketing mix. Carriers with higher common ownership tended to deliver lower service quality and charge higher prices. The effect was weaker for firms with high customer-asset value and stronger among rivals that compete head-to-head across many markets.
studies.why_it_matters: It connects an abstract corporate-finance phenomenon to the things consumers actually feel — price and service — and gives regulators and investors a marketing-side indicator of softened competition.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your category has concentrated institutional ownership, treat customer-asset value as a defense: the study suggests firms with strong customer equity resist the service-quality slide, which makes the case for protecting experience investment when competitive pressure eases.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Those index funds in your retirement account may own several of the airlines you choose between — and this research suggests that overlap tracks with pricier tickets and thinner service.
studies.caveats: Single industry (U.S. airlines) and single country; observational panel data, so causality is inferred rather than experimentally established; service quality measured through available industry metrics.
studies.verdict_notes: Dataset (U.S. airlines, 1995-2025), direction of effects and both moderators (attenuated by customer-asset value, amplified for multi-market rivals) all match; caveats correctly flag the observational panel design.

studies.title: Fixing a Bad Meal? Compensate the Friend Too — but Only in the Right Dose
studies.paper_title: When recovery goes beyond the focal customer: service recovery in customer-companion contexts
studies.the_study: Three experiments with loyalty program customers tested how people respond to service recovery when they were with a companion. Customers reacted more favorably to recovery when a companion was present than when dining or traveling alone, and when companion presence was held constant, including the companion in the compensation worked best for low-tier members when the payout was small and for high-tier members when it was large. Recovery satisfaction and "felt status" both explained the effect.
studies.why_it_matters: Most compensation policies treat the complaining customer as a solo actor; this suggests that who else is at the table changes the return on the same dollar of recovery.
studies.story_angle_primary: Test tier-contingent recovery rules: small gestures extended to the whole party for ordinary members, larger exclusive-feeling gestures for top-tier guests — and track whether including companions changes repurchase and referral, not just satisfaction scores.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Complaining in front of a friend isn't just awkward — the research suggests you're likely to come away happier with the apology than if you'd been alone, especially if the business makes the gesture to both of you.
studies.caveats: Scenario-based experiments measuring responses to hypothetical encounters rather than observed behavior after real failures; loyalty program context; sample composition and sizes not reported in the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: Three experiments, the companion-presence effect, the tier x compensation-amount interaction and both mechanisms are reported correctly; only the consumption setting is embellished beyond the abstract.

studies.title: Asking Service Staff to Sell: Whether It Energizes or Burns Them Out Depends on the Climate You Set
studies.paper_title: Service–Sales Ambidexterity as a Double-Edged Sword: Dual-Path Effects of Frontline Employee Appraisals on Performance
studies.the_study: A field study of frontline employees plus a complementary experiment examined how workers interpret the demand to both serve and sell. Employees in a "promotion" psychological climate appraised the dual role as a challenge, which raised work engagement and performance; those in a "prevention" climate appraised it as a hindrance, which drove burnout and lower performance. Finding meaning in serving customers amplified the upside and buffered the downside.
studies.why_it_matters: Companies increasingly bolt sales targets onto service roles; this suggests identical job designs produce opposite performance outcomes depending on how management frames risk, error and growth.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before adding sales quotas to service teams, examine whether your climate signals opportunity or error-avoidance — and consider whether reinforcing the meaning of customer service is a cheaper performance lever than incentive redesign.
studies.story_angle_secondary: That awkward moment when a helpful service rep pivots into a pitch often reflects pressure from above; the same employee can sound enthusiastic or exhausted depending entirely on how their workplace frames the task.
studies.caveats: Field portion is correlational with self-reported climate and appraisals; the causal evidence comes from a complementary experiment; sample size, industry and country not specified in the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: Dual-path mechanism (promotion/challenge/engagement vs prevention/hindrance/burnout), the work-meaningfulness moderator and the division of labour between field study and complementary experiment are all represented correctly.

studies.title: Devout Customers Reported More Willingness to Be Rude to Staff — Unless Karma Was on Their Minds
studies.paper_title: Belief, forgiveness and karma: unpacking customer incivility following service failures
studies.the_study: Three studies (n=202 restaurant scenario, n=279 hotel scenario, n=297 Prolific experiment) tested how religious belief relates to customer incivility after a service failure. Stronger religious belief was associated with greater incivility intentions toward frontline employees, operating through lower situational forgiveness of the employee. That pathway was weaker among people with strong belief in karma, and weaker still when karma-style action–consequence thinking was made salient experimentally.
studies.why_it_matters: It identifies a customer-side predictor of frontline abuse that firms never measure, and shows that priming consequence-thinking — not moralizing about belief — can soften it.
studies.story_angle_primary: Rather than profiling customers, test neutral, universal conduct statements and recovery designs that actively invite forgiveness of the individual employee, and pair them with real escalation routes and supervisor backup for staff absorbing the abuse.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A counterintuitive finding about who lashes out at waitstaff: self-reported piety didn't predict more forgiveness of the person serving you — but thinking about how your actions come back around did.
studies.caveats: Hypothetical scenarios and stated intentions rather than observed behavior; online panel (Prolific) in Study 3; the first two studies are cross-sectional associations; findings limited to the specific beliefs, contexts and intention measures tested.
studies.verdict_notes: Samples (202/279/297), mediator and karma boundary condition all match; one phrase implies a comparison of effect size across studies that the abstract does not make.

studies.title: Not all workplace stress is bad: the kind that makes staff steal — and the kind that stops them
studies.paper_title: Can Stress Curb Unethical Employee Behavior? Evidence From Frontline Contexts
studies.the_study: Across three studies with 708 frontline service employees, researchers separated "challenge" stressors (demanding work that offers a route to achievement and growth) from "hindrance" stressors (red tape, blocked progress, barriers). Challenge stressors were associated with *less* unethical behavior — theft, service sabotage, cutting corners — while hindrance stressors were associated with more. The mechanism was self-efficacy: challenging demands raised employees' belief in their own competence, hindrances eroded it. Self-directed development activity moderated both effects; peer-led development only buffered challenge stressors.
studies.why_it_matters: Service firms lose real money to employee theft and deliberate service sabotage, and the standard response is to reduce pressure across the board. This evidence suggests the type of pressure matters more than the amount — and that removing bureaucratic friction may do more for ethics than lightening the workload.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audit your frontline stressors by type, not volume: test whether removing hindrance stressors (approval bottlenecks, conflicting policies, unclear authority) reduces shrinkage and sabotage more than cutting targets does. Worth treating as a hypothesis to pilot in a few stores or call centers before rolling out, since the evidence here is employee self-report rather than observed theft data.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It reframes a familiar workplace experience: the exhausting-but-meaningful shift and the exhausting-but-pointless one are not the same kind of tired, and the second one is the one that corrodes people's sense of competence.
studies.caveats: Relies on employee-reported measures of unethical behavior rather than observed misconduct; study designs and countries not specified in the abstract; self-efficacy mechanism inferred from mediation rather than manipulated directly.
studies.verdict_notes: 708 employees across three studies, the challenge/hindrance split, the self-efficacy mechanism and the two moderators are reported correctly; the direction attributed to the peer-led development moderator is not stated in the abstract.

studies.title: Customers find humanoid service robots creepy — except when the service is embarrassing
studies.paper_title: Aye robot! When should(n’t) service providers say yes to humanoid robot frontline employees?
studies.journal: The Journal of Marketing Theory and Practice
studies.the_study: Two experiments compared customer reactions to humanoid robot versus human frontline employees. Robots were rated lower on warmth and higher on "creepiness," which reduced customer comfort, lowered service expectations and dampened intentions to use the service. The exception was service contexts involving embarrassment: there, the human employee's own creepiness rating rose with the context while the robot's did not, narrowing or reversing the robot's disadvantage.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives service operators a selection rule rather than a blanket verdict on robots: deploy them where human presence is itself the source of discomfort, not as a general substitute at the counter.
studies.story_angle_primary: Map your service touchpoints by customer embarrassment before deciding where humanoid robots go — pharmacy pickups, intimate-product retail, screening and intake conversations are candidate tests, while warmth-dependent hospitality moments are not. Because these are controlled experiments rather than deployments, treat the embarrassment boundary condition as something to validate in a live pilot with actual usage and satisfaction data.
studies.story_angle_secondary: There is a reason some people prefer the self-checkout or the app for certain purchases: the discomfort of being seen by another human can outweigh the coldness of a machine.
studies.caveats: Two experimental studies only; design, sample size and recruitment source not specified in the abstract; outcomes are behavioral intentions and perceptions rather than observed service use; "humanoid robot" likely presented via scenario or stimulus rather than real interaction.
studies.verdict_notes: Two studies, the warmth/creepiness/comfort/intentions chain and the embarrassment boundary condition match; the described direction and magnitude of the human-employee creepiness shift goes beyond the abstract.

studies.title: Gluten-free shoppers aren't asking for more choice — they want bread that tastes good and is safe
studies.paper_title: Consumer satisfaction drivers in the Portuguese gluten-free food market: the role of product quality, service quality and assortment variety
studies.the_study: A survey of 444 Portuguese consumers of gluten-free products tested which factors track with satisfaction, using correlation and multiple regression. Product quality was the strongest correlate of satisfaction, followed by service quality and then assortment variety. Safety (freedom from cross-contamination) and taste were the most valued product attributes, and respondents reported clear dissatisfaction with availability in specific categories: bread, pastry and ready-to-eat meals.
studies.why_it_matters: In a fast-growing specialty food segment, retailers and manufacturers often compete on range expansion; this suggests the satisfaction payoff sits more in quality assurance and in filling a few specific, still-poorly-served categories.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you sell into the gluten-free segment, test depth over breadth — reformulation and contamination-control credentials in bread, pastry and ready meals may move satisfaction more than adding SKUs. Note this is one national market and self-reported satisfaction, so treat the category gaps as a research prompt for your own assortment and sales data.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For anyone shopping gluten-free, the study puts numbers on a common complaint: the shelf keeps getting longer but the bread aisle and the ready-meal cabinet still disappoint.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey, so no causal claims; single country (Portugal); perceptual measures with acknowledged risk of construct overlap; stated satisfaction rather than observed purchasing.
studies.verdict_notes: N=444, method and the ranking of satisfaction drivers match; the headline's "aren't asking for more choice" sits awkwardly against the abstract's finding of dissatisfaction with limited availability, and the cross-contamination gloss is added.

studies.title: How close the disaster feels decides whether tourists boycott a destination
studies.paper_title: The effect of service failure crisis in destinations on tourism boycotts: The moderating role of power distance beliefs
studies.the_study: Two experiments grounded in construal level theory tested how the "scope" of a service failure crisis at a travel destination — whether it happened to the respondent personally, to someone in their community, or to a stranger elsewhere — affects their willingness to boycott that destination. Boycott intentions were strongest for personally experienced failures, weaker for failures within one's own social circle, and weakest for distant, external cases. The effect ran through a chain of perceived relative deprivation (a sense of being treated unfairly compared with others) and then eroded trust in the destination, and was amplified among people with high power distance beliefs.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives destination marketers and service recovery teams a triage logic: the same incident carries very different reputational cost depending on how socially close the audience feels to the victim, and the damage operates through felt unfairness rather than the failure itself.
studies.story_angle_primary: Crisis response playbooks usually grade incidents by severity; this work suggests grading them by social proximity to the audience too, and testing recovery messages that attack the sense of being unfairly treated — not just the operational fault. Because these are scenario experiments, treat the hierarchy as a hypothesis to validate against real booking and cancellation data.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It helps explain why a travel horror story that happened to a friend changes your plans while an identical story in the news barely registers — and why the sting is less about the incident than about feeling you got a worse deal than other travelers.
studies.caveats: Two scenario-based experiments rather than observed travel behavior; stated boycott intentions; sample details and country context not reported in the abstract; cultural moderator (power distance beliefs) measured, not manipulated at the country level.
studies.verdict_notes: Two experiments, the personal > communal > external hierarchy, the serial mediation and the power-distance moderator are all accurate; the "Why it matters" line overstates what mediation shows and the digest drops self-bias theory.

studies.title: For small-business clients, getting the order right beats having the slickest logistics tech
studies.paper_title: Logistics Service Quality on Customer Satisfaction and Repurchase Intention: Evidence from Thai SMEs
studies.the_study: Researchers surveyed 236 Thai small and medium-sized enterprises about their logistics service providers, testing how logistics service quality feeds customer satisfaction and repurchase intention using structural equation modeling. Logistics service quality influenced repurchase both directly and through satisfaction. The notable detail: core operational basics — order accuracy and the quality of contact with staff — mattered more to SME satisfaction than technological sophistication or the provider's corporate image.
studies.why_it_matters: Logistics and B2B service providers often market digital tracking dashboards and brand credentials to small-business buyers, while this evidence points to fulfillment accuracy and the human account contact as the real retention levers.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audit what your SME clients actually rate you on: test whether reallocating spend from platform features and brand campaigns into order accuracy and named human contacts moves repurchase rates. Note this is a single-country cross-sectional survey, so treat it as a prompt for a controlled service-level test rather than proof.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A useful reminder of what small-business owners value in their suppliers: reliability and a person who picks up the phone, not a fancier app.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey, cannot establish causation; stated repurchase intention rather than observed renewals; single country (Thailand); self-reported data from one respondent per firm with common method bias addressed only via Harman's single-factor test.
studies.verdict_notes: N=236 Thai SMEs, SEM, direct plus satisfaction-mediated effects on repurchase intention, and the primacy of order accuracy and personnel contact over technology and corporate image all match; Harman's single-factor test correctly noted in caveats.

studies.title: Corner shops can win the speed game without any of the quick-commerce infrastructure
studies.paper_title: Competing through quick commerce: evidence from urban nanostores
studies.journal: International Journal of Retail & Distribution Management
studies.the_study: A survey of 340 consumers across 60 urban "nanostores" — tiny independent neighborhood shops — in Bandung, Indonesia tested what makes shoppers see these micro-retailers as competitive against quick-commerce platforms. Convenience, satisfaction with delivery, and basic digital service quality (chat ordering and similar lightweight tools) all strengthened perceived competitiveness, which in turn lifted purchase intention on both product and price grounds. Perceived competitiveness carried the effects of convenience and delivery satisfaction, but digital service quality worked directly on shoppers rather than through any sense of relative advantage.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes quick commerce as a perception of immediacy that proximity and a WhatsApp order can deliver, rather than something only dark stores and fleet algorithms can buy — with implications for platforms competing in dense informal retail markets.
studies.story_angle_primary: If perceived immediacy rather than logistics scale drives choice, platforms and FMCG brands in emerging markets should test partnering with, rather than displacing, neighborhood stores — and test how little digital tooling is needed to make a shop feel "instant." Survey-based, single-city evidence, so validate with actual order data before building strategy on it.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For shoppers, the fastest option is often the shop around the corner with a messaging app — and the feeling of speed, more than literal delivery minutes, is what drives where we buy.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey analyzed with PLS-SEM, cannot establish causation; stated purchase intention rather than observed purchases; single city in one developing economy; consumers sampled at stores, risking selection toward existing customers.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, sample and mediation pattern all match the abstract; two small embellishments (the "chat ordering" example and the "feeling of speed beats delivery minutes" claim) go slightly past what the abstract states.

studies.title: When your hashtag gets hijacked, the angriest posts aren't the ones that spread
studies.paper_title: The Dark Side of #Engagement: A Multi-Method Study of Negative eWOM Diffusion in Bashtag Networks Through Dual Factor Theory
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed 14,511 social media posts tied to two famously hijacked brand hashtag campaigns — McDonald's and Walkers Crisps — using LDA topic modeling and VADER sentiment analysis, then surveyed 418 social media users about what makes them pass such content along. They built a typology (REACTS) of the narratives consumers tell inside "bashtag" networks, and identified the enablers and inhibitors of negative word-of-mouth diffusion. Counter to the well-established negativity effect, the most negative messages did not spread further once a conversation was already negatively skewed.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests a hijacked hashtag is not an automatic death spiral: within an already hostile thread, extra outrage loses its marginal shock value, which changes the calculus on when and how hard to intervene.
studies.story_angle_primary: Social and brand teams can use this to question the reflex of treating every negative spike as equally contagious — the data hint that diffusion depends on the surrounding sentiment mix, not just message valence. Worth building monitoring that tracks the composition of a hashtag conversation, not only its volume, and testing proactive response playbooks before a campaign hashtag launches.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For anyone who has piled onto a brand hashtag: the research maps the recognizable genres of consumer complaint-posting, and finds that in a pile-on, the harshest takes often get lost in the noise rather than becoming the ones everyone shares.
studies.caveats: Two brands and two campaigns in a single market context; the survey component (N=418) relies on self-reported sharing intentions rather than observed sharing; sentiment tools like VADER approximate tone imperfectly, especially with sarcasm, which is the native language of bashtags.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample sizes, methods and the counter-negativity finding match; the digest states the diffusion result slightly more firmly than the abstract's hedged wording, and the "single market context" caveat is questionable for a US/UK brand pair.

studies.title: What a million words of app-store griping reveals about fintech users' well-being
studies.paper_title: Beyond continuance: how FinTech app experiences shape user well-being
studies.the_study: Instead of surveying users, the researchers mined unsolicited Arabic and English reviews of digital wallet apps from the Google Play Store and Apple App Store in Saudi Arabia, using a pipeline of hierarchical clustering, topic modeling, sentiment analysis, machine classification with human validation, and Ridge/Lasso regression. Four experiential factors emerged: complaint handling effectiveness, perceived system reliability, information ambiguity, and user autonomy. Effective complaint handling, reliability, and autonomy were linked to higher user well-being; ambiguous information — unclear fees, statuses, error messages — was linked to lower well-being.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes the fintech scorecard from "will they keep using it" to "does using it make people feel better or worse," and names unclear communication as an actively harmful design choice rather than a minor annoyance.
studies.story_angle_primary: App and service leaders can treat their own review corpus as a standing customer-experience instrument — the method shown here extracts measurable constructs from feedback they already own. The practical test: audit where your product leaves users uncertain about what just happened to their money, and whether complaint resolution is resourced as a well-being lever rather than a cost center.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The thing that most erodes trust in a payment app isn't a missing feature — it's not knowing whether your transfer went through, what a fee is for, or who to ask. Readers may recognize that the apps they tolerate and the apps they resent differ mainly in how clearly they explain themselves.
studies.caveats: Single country (Saudi Arabia) and a single app category; app-store reviewers are a self-selected, extreme-opinion sample; well-being is inferred from review text rather than measured directly; regression on observational data cannot establish causation.
studies.verdict_notes: Method pipeline, the four experiential factors and the direction of each effect all match; only the headline's "million words" figure is unsupported.

studies.title: Rude customers make staff less caring — and the boss's favorites take it hardest
studies.paper_title: How customer incivility reduces employees’ compassionate service behaviors: the exacerbating role of leader–member exchange
studies.the_study: Researchers ran a four-wave, time-lagged survey of 316 customer-facing service employees in the United States, recruited via Prolific, to trace how customer incivility affects "compassionate service behavior" — the small acts of care frontline staff extend to customers. Incivility eroded compassionate behavior indirectly, by raising employees' sense of workplace uncertainty. The twist: the damage was strongest among employees with high-quality relationships with their managers (high leader–member exchange), apparently because uncertainty is a bigger shock to people used to relational clarity and predictability.
studies.why_it_matters: Abusive customers don't just hurt morale, they degrade the very warmth that service brands sell — and the usual managerial remedy, strong manager–employee bonds, may not buffer it the way leadership playbooks assume.
studies.story_angle_primary: Service leaders could test whether their customer-incivility response protocols actually reduce felt uncertainty — clear escalation rules, explicit backing for staff who disengage from abusive customers — rather than assuming a good manager relationship inoculates the team. This is survey evidence from one national sample, so treat the high-LMX finding as a hypothesis to probe in your own staff data, not a settled fact.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Snapping at a cashier or support agent doesn't just ruin one interaction: the evidence suggests it quietly drains the employee's capacity to be kind to the next several customers in line.
studies.caveats: Online panel (Prolific) self-report across four waves rather than observed service behavior; single country (US); correlational design despite time lags, so causality is inferred, not proven.
studies.verdict_notes: Design (four-wave Prolific survey, N=316, US), the uncertainty mediator and the exacerbating high-LMX moderation are all reported correctly, and the correlational caveat is present; only the consumer-facing "next several customers" line overreaches.

studies.title: Speed is a luxury killer: what 1.2 million Google reviews say about AI in high-end service
studies.paper_title: AI is not for luxury: balancing Chronos efficiency and Kairos experience
studies.journal: International Journal of Quality and Service Sciences
studies.the_study: Using a corpus of 1.2 million Google Maps reviews across 10 luxury chains, researchers hand-coded 2,000 reviews and compared that human coding against an automated large language model (Gemini) extraction, looking specifically at how customers talk about time. They find recurring "temporal fractures" where AI-driven acceleration delivers efficiency but strips out relational time — the unhurried attention that justifies premium pricing — and sort brands into five positions on an efficiency-versus-experience frontier (Decelerator, Bifurcator, Autonomy Provider, Fragmentor, Automator). Notably, the automated LLM pass missed what the authors call "Kairos deficits," failing to distinguish deliberate slowness from service failure.
studies.why_it_matters: It puts customer language behind a suspicion many premium operators have: automation gains that look free on the P&L can be billed to trust, loyalty and price premium, where no one is measuring.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before rolling out the next automation in a premium channel, consider separating journeys where customers want speed from those where waiting is the product — and note the methodological warning that an LLM reading your review pile may not flag the difference between intentional pacing and a broken experience.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If a high-end hotel, restaurant or store feels oddly brisk and transactional now, you're not imagining it — and reviewers are describing exactly that loss in their own words.
studies.caveats: Review text is self-selected and skews to extremes; only 2,000 of 1.2 million reviews were human-coded; the archetype framework is interpretive and derived from the data rather than independently tested; confined to luxury chains with Google Maps presence; heavy conceptual vocabulary built on a modest coded sample.
studies.verdict_notes: Corpus size, dual-coding design, the five archetypes and the LLM's failure to detect Kairos deficits all match the abstract, and the caveats already flag that only 2,000 reviews were human-coded and that the archetypes are interpretive.

studies.title: Foreign-branded universities: students say the country ties matter more than the price
studies.paper_title: Students’ choice of university in transnational education: the factors influencing their decision to study at a country-branded university
studies.journal: Journal of Marketing for HIGHER EDUCATION
studies.the_study: An online survey of 1,199 students enrolled at Canadian-, Chinese- and US-affiliated universities located in Bangladesh, Egypt and the United Arab Emirates asked what drove their choice of a "country-branded university." Institutional reputation, perceived service quality, country brand authenticity and financial factors each influenced at least 70% of respondents. In all three institutions, country brand authenticity outranked financial factors — nearly three-quarters of students cited genuine ties to the foreign country as a reason for enrolling.
studies.why_it_matters: For the fast-growing transnational education market, it suggests the borrowed national brand is a core product attribute, not decoration — and that students are watching whether the foreign connection is real.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your brand licenses or borrows a country identity, the finding implies the authenticity of that link — faculty, curriculum, degree parity, actual institutional involvement — may be worth more in recruitment messaging than tuition discounting; a hypothesis worth testing in enrollment data.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Families weighing an overseas-branded campus at home should ask what the foreign affiliation concretely delivers, because students in this study were buying the authenticity of that tie as much as the education.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey of stated, retrospective reasons rather than observed choice behavior; three host countries and three affiliated institutions only; cannot establish causation; results are largely descriptive percentages.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample (N=1,199), host and affiliate countries, the "at least 70 per cent" figure and country brand authenticity outranking financial factors are all reproduced correctly, and the descriptive, non-causal nature is flagged.

studies.title: Faith-aligned features won't save a glitchy app: evidence from Islamic mobile banking reviews
studies.paper_title: Are Islamic features enough to fulfil ethical service expectations? Insights from customer emotions in mobile banking
studies.the_study: Researchers applied lexicon-based text mining to customer reviews of Islamic mobile banking apps in Indonesia and built panel data regression models linking service dimensions and expressed emotions to satisfaction. Ease of use, convenience, perceived usefulness and adherence to Islamic attributes all contributed to satisfaction, while negative emotions in reviews dragged it down. The practical upshot: complaints clustered around system updates, verification processes, core banking functionality and stability — basic reliability, not religious compliance.
studies.why_it_matters: Values-based positioning raises expectations of service parity rather than excusing shortfalls; customers appear to treat competent, reliable execution as part of the ethical promise.
studies.story_angle_primary: For any brand built on a values proposition — faith-based, ethical, sustainable — this is a prompt to audit whether operational basics meet mainstream category standards, since the review data suggest a failed login can read to customers as a broken promise.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It's a reminder that what people actually write in app reviews is mostly about things working, even when they chose the app for its principles.
studies.caveats: Single country (Indonesia) and single category; app-review text is self-selected and skews toward extremes; lexicon-based sentiment coding is approximate; associational models, not causal.
studies.verdict_notes: Method (lexicon-based text mining plus panel regression, Indonesia) and the satisfaction drivers match; the claim that complaints "clustered" around four specific areas restates a managerial recommendation as a frequency finding.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**

- **Frontline staff remain the gating variable — now on the labor side, not just the technology side.** The previous run's "When the AI is wrong, frontline staff stop thinking like customers" (W7214671269) established that governance and discretion decide whether service tech pays off. Three new studies extend the same logic to job design: "Asking Service Staff to Sell: Whether It Energizes or Burns Them Out Depends on the Climate You Set" (W7221728768), "Not all workplace stress is bad" (W7221898122) and "Rude customers make staff less caring — and the boss's favorites take it hardest" (W7220440663) all find that identical demands produce opposite outcomes depending on how they are framed, bounded and backed up.
- **Large language models reading customer feedback miss the relational layer.** "Speed is a luxury killer" (W7220919414) reports that an automated LLM pass failed to distinguish deliberate slowness from service failure — the same shortfall documented last run in "ChatGPT and HR managers read the same guest complaints" (W7214601318), where the model was strong on operational pattern recognition and thin on interactional repair.
- **Review and complaint corpora are consolidating into the default CX measurement instrument.** "What a million words of app-store griping reveals about fintech users' well-being" (W7222527276), "Faith-aligned features won't save a glitchy app" (W7216405737), W7220919414 and the 141,000-complaint analysis (W7204606942) continue the method established last run by "There is no universal recipe for good service" (W7202253581) and the halal luxury hotel review study (W7203443165).
- **Luxury service is being hollowed out by its own growth and efficiency plays.** W7220919414 finds automation strips the unhurried "relational time" that justifies premium pricing, sitting directly alongside the previous digest's "reversed conspicuousness" finding in luxury brand extensions (W7214625896).
- **Humanoid interfaces still carry a penalty.** "Customers find humanoid service robots creepy" (W7220660112) echoes "The more human your AI looks, the harder customers fall when it fails" (W7204275888) and "When a service robot fumbles, the customers watching are the ones who walk away" (W7203866299).

**Advances**

- **Robot deployment gets a boundary condition.** Where the previous batch established the anthropomorphism penalty, W7220660112 identifies where it reverses: in embarrassing service contexts the human employee's own creepiness rating rises while the robot's does not — a selection rule rather than a blanket verdict.
- **Recovery triage extends from channel to social context and loyalty tier.** "Fixing a Bad Meal? Compensate the Friend Too" (W7221159140) adds companion presence and tier-contingent payout size to the triage logic previously built on failure severity and remedy type (W7201883691, W7203609438).
- **Crisis attribution moves from who spreads it to how close it feels.** "How close the disaster feels decides whether tourists boycott a destination" (W7221524554) adds social proximity and felt relative deprivation to the attribution work in "In an online firestorm, it's the obsessives who spread the damage" (W7213665568) and "When AI fails customers, apologize" (W7172201743). "When your hashtag gets hijacked, the angriest posts aren't the ones that spread" (W7206212528) pushes further, finding the negativity effect breaks down inside already-hostile threads.
- **Service exclusion acquires a quantitative anchor.** The previous run's qualitative thread — the self-checkout efficiency paradox (W7197051994) and disabled customers' dignity accounts (W7204466776) — is now matched by W7204606942, which links comprehension and action burden to dispute escalation in economically disadvantaged areas across 141,251 complaints.

**Counterpoints**

- **Transparency is being reframed rather than rejected.** The previous batch suggested less communication can be safer ("When a package is late, saying nothing may protect the retailer," W7172357977) and that more tracking detail yields little for hurried shoppers (W7212038717). The new evidence shifts the variable: W7222527276 names information ambiguity — unclear fees, statuses, error messages — as actively harmful to well-being, and W7204606942 finds comprehension and the ability to act, not disclosure volume, predict escalation. The question is becoming clarity, not quantity.
- **Values-based segments may need fewer bespoke attributes than last run implied.** The halal luxury hotel review study (W7203443165) surfaced service-quality themes distinctive to the faith-based setting; W7216405737 finds complaints about Islamic mobile banking cluster on logins, verification and stability rather than religious compliance, suggesting values positioning raises expectations of category-standard execution rather than creating a separate scorecard.

**New themes**

- **Market structure as a customer-experience variable.** "When Rival Airlines Share the Same Big Investors, Service Gets Worse and Fares Go Up" (W7223706258) brings common ownership — a corporate-finance phenomenon — into the marketing mix, with no precedent in the previous digest.
- **Customer-side predictors of frontline abuse.** "Devout Customers Reported More Willingness to Be Rude to Staff — Unless Karma Was on Their Minds" (W7223658951) opens a line the previous run only addressed from the employee side.
- **Informal and micro-retail competing with quick commerce.** "Corner shops can win the speed game without any of the quick-commerce infrastructure" (W7215042272) is a new emerging-market retail thread.
- **B2B and specialty-category basics.** "For small-business clients, getting the order right beats having the slickest logistics tech" (W7215042510) and "Gluten-free shoppers aren't asking for more choice" (W7222470326) both argue against feature and assortment expansion in favor of execution — new territory for this topic.
- **Borrowed national brands as a product attribute.** "Foreign-branded universities" (W7221546035) introduces country brand authenticity as a service-choice driver.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Four studies in this batch converge on the same unmeasured input to customer experience — the condition of the people delivering it. Customer incivility eroded staff capacity for compassionate service through felt uncertainty, and hit employees with the strongest manager relationships hardest ("Rude customers make staff less caring," W7220440663); bolting sales targets onto service roles energized or burned out identical workers depending on whether management framed risk as opportunity or error ("Asking Service Staff to Sell," W7221728768); the type of pressure, not the amount, predicted theft and service sabotage, with bureaucratic friction the corrosive kind ("Not all workplace stress is bad," W7221898122); and one of the clearest predictors of abuse directed at staff turned out to be a customer trait no firm tracks ("Devout Customers Reported More Willingness to Be Rude to Staff," W7223658951).

**Why pitch this now:** Retailers, banks and hospitality groups are simultaneously adding sales quotas and AI tools to shrinking frontline teams, reporting shrinkage as a board-level problem, and describing customer abuse as a retention crisis — and this evidence says those three stories are the same story.

**Angle:** A reported feature on the frontline as an uncosted line item in the experience economy: how abusive customers, badly framed dual roles and approval bottlenecks quietly produce the thin, transactional service brands then try to fix with technology. For CX, operations and HR leaders, with a general-interest version on what rudeness at the counter actually does to the next person in line.

**Potential headlines:**
- Abusive customers measurably reduce how kindly staff treat everyone after them
- Pointless paperwork, not hard targets, is what pushes frontline staff to cut corners
- Your shrinkage problem might be a job-design problem

**Potential outlets:**
- **Retail Dive** — covers frontline labor, shrinkage and store operations as linked problems, which is exactly the connection the stressor-type evidence makes.
- **MIT Sloan Management Review** — the climate-and-appraisal findings are a job-design argument for managers, with a clean testable prescription rather than a general plea for kindness.
- **Restaurant Business** — hospitality operators are the readers living the customer-abuse and tip-era civility problem, and the companion-compensation and incivility work both land in their rooms.
- **Vox** — strong on everyday social behavior explained through research, and the "who lashes out at waitstaff, and what actually curbs it" material is a natural consumer-facing piece.
pitch_ideas_raw:
- **What 141,000 Consumer Complaints Reveal About Why Disputes Escalate in Poorer Neighborhoods (Work ID W7204606942):** Disputes track with whether consumers can understand and act on a remedy rather than the size of the loss, which makes disclosure-heavy recovery a misdiagnosis in financial services, for a personal-finance column or a financial-services trade feature.
- **When Rival Airlines Share the Same Big Investors, Service Gets Worse and Fares Go Up (Work ID W7223706258):** Thirty years of U.S. airline data linking overlapping institutional ownership to higher fares and thinner service, with customer-asset value as the apparent defense, for a business or antitrust-focused general-interest piece.
- **Fixing a Bad Meal? Compensate the Friend Too (Work ID W7221159140):** Loyalty tier plus who else is at the table changes the return on the same recovery dollar — small gestures to the whole party for ordinary members, larger exclusive ones for top tiers, for a hospitality trade explainer or a loyalty-marketing brief.
- **Asking Service Staff to Sell (Work ID W7221728768):** The same sell-and-serve mandate produces engagement or burnout depending on whether the workplace climate signals growth or error-avoidance, for a CMO- or COO-audience column on sales targets in service roles.
- **Devout Customers Reported More Willingness to Be Rude to Staff (Work ID W7223658951):** Self-reported piety tracked with less forgiveness of the individual employee, while karma-style consequence thinking softened it — a counterintuitive consumer-psychology explainer for a general-interest outlet.
- **Not all workplace stress is bad (Work ID W7221898122):** Challenge stressors were associated with less theft and sabotage while red tape was associated with more, which argues for clearing bottlenecks before cutting targets, for a retail operations or loss-prevention trade feature.
- **Customers find humanoid service robots creepy — except when the service is embarrassing (Work ID W7220660112):** A deployment rule instead of a verdict — put robots where human presence is itself the discomfort, such as pharmacy pickup or intake, for a retail-technology trade explainer.
- **Gluten-free shoppers aren't asking for more choice (Work ID W7222470326):** Quality and contamination safety outranked assortment breadth, with bread, pastry and ready meals named as the still-failing categories, for a grocery or food-industry trade brief.
- **How close the disaster feels decides whether tourists boycott a destination (Work ID W7221524554):** Crisis playbooks grade incidents by severity; this grades them by social proximity to the audience and routes the damage through felt unfairness, for a travel trade outlet or a crisis-communications column.
- **For small-business clients, getting the order right beats having the slickest logistics tech (Work ID W7215042510):** SME buyers rated order accuracy and a named human contact above tracking platforms and brand credentials, for a B2B logistics or supply-chain trade brief.
- **Corner shops can win the speed game without any of the quick-commerce infrastructure (Work ID W7215042272):** Perceived immediacy, deliverable with proximity and a chat app, rivals dark-store logistics in dense urban markets, for a retail trade feature on quick commerce in emerging markets.
- **When your hashtag gets hijacked, the angriest posts aren't the ones that spread (Work ID W7206212528):** Within an already hostile thread, extra outrage loses its marginal shock value — a challenge to treating every negative spike as equally contagious, for a PR or social-marketing trade outlet.
- **What a million words of app-store griping reveals about fintech users' well-being (Work ID W7222527276):** Unclear fees, statuses and error messages are an active harm, not a minor annoyance, and complaint handling reads as a well-being lever rather than a cost center, for a fintech trade outlet or a consumer-money column.
- **Rude customers make staff less caring — and the boss's favorites take it hardest (Work ID W7220440663):** The surprise is that strong manager relationships amplified rather than buffered the damage, which undercuts the standard leadership remedy, for a management or HR-focused column.
- **Speed is a luxury killer (Work ID W7220919414):** Reviewers describe premium brands trading relational time for efficiency, and the LLM reading the reviews couldn't tell intentional pacing from a broken experience, for a luxury business feature or a data-and-measurement piece for analytics-minded readers.
- **Foreign-branded universities: students say the country ties matter more than the price (Work ID W7221546035):** Country brand authenticity outranked financial factors across three host markets, making the realness of the affiliation a recruitment asset rather than decoration, for a higher-education trade outlet.
- **Faith-aligned features won't save a glitchy app (Work ID W7216405737):** For any values-based brand, a failed login reads as a broken promise — complaints clustered on stability and verification, not religious compliance, for a brand-strategy column or a fintech trade brief.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: Marketing Research Digest — Customer Experience & Service — 2026-10-29
**Checked:** 2026-10-29 | **Studies reviewed:** 17
**Primary audience:** marketers and brand leaders | **Secondary audience:** general readers and consumers

---

### Study 1: What 141,000 Consumer Complaints Reveal About Why Disputes Escalate in Poorer Neighborhoods
**Work ID:** W7204606942 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Comparison not tested** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "It suggests that in financial services, disputes are driven less by the failure itself than by whether people can comprehend and act on the remedy"
- **Abstract says:** "we examine how seven salience dimensions relate to dispute escalation. The results suggest that cognitive-control and behavioral-control salience have the strongest positive associations with disputing."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports relative strength among seven control-salience dimensions, not a contest between the service failure itself and control cues; the digest implies the failure's role was measured and found weaker.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to "among the control-related cues examined, comprehension and ability to act were the strongest correlates of escalation," dropping the implied comparison with the failure itself."

### Study 2: When Rival Airlines Share the Same Big Investors, Service Gets Worse and Fares Go Up
**Work ID:** W7223706258 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 3: Fixing a Bad Meal? Compensate the Friend Too — but Only in the Right Dose
**Work ID:** W7221159140 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Service context not specified** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Customers reacted more favorably to recovery when a companion was present than when dining or traveling alone"
- **Abstract says:** "Across three experiments, this study examines loyalty program customers' responses to service recovery in social consumption settings. ... Customers responded more favorably to recovery in companion-accompanied than in solo consumption contexts."
- **Problem:** The abstract says only "social consumption settings"; the specific dining/travel framing (and the "Bad Meal" headline) is not verifiable from the abstract.
- **Suggested fix:** "Refer to "companion-accompanied versus solo consumption settings" and note that the specific service contexts are not identified in the abstract."

### Study 4: Asking Service Staff to Sell: Whether It Energizes or Burns Them Out Depends on the Climate You Set
**Work ID:** W7221728768 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 5: Devout Customers Reported More Willingness to Be Rude to Staff — Unless Karma Was on Their Minds
**Work ID:** W7223658951 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Implied cross-study comparison** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "That pathway was weaker among people with strong belief in karma, and weaker still when karma-style action–consequence thinking was made salient experimentally."
- **Abstract says:** "In Study 2, this indirect association was weaker among customers reporting stronger belief in karma. In Study 3, it was weaker when karma-related considerations were made situationally salient."
- **Problem:** "Weaker still" suggests the experimental manipulation attenuated the pathway more than measured karma belief did; the abstract reports two separate attenuations in different studies with no comparison between them.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to "and also weaker when karma-style action–consequence thinking was made salient in a separate experiment.""

### Study 6: Not all workplace stress is bad: the kind that makes staff steal — and the kind that stops them
**Work ID:** W7221898122 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Moderator direction unverifiable** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "peer-led development only buffered challenge stressors"
- **Abstract says:** "Self-led development moderates both stressor types, while peer-led development only affects challenge stressors."
- **Problem:** The abstract states only that peer-led development moderates the challenge-stressor path, without specifying whether it strengthens or dampens it; "buffered" asserts a dampening direction and sits oddly with challenge stressors having a beneficial effect.
- **Suggested fix:** "Write "peer-led development moderated only the challenge-stressor path (direction not specified in the abstract).""

### Study 7: Customers find humanoid service robots creepy — except when the service is embarrassing
**Work ID:** W7220660112 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Boundary-condition detail beyond abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "there, the human employee's own creepiness rating rose with the context while the robot's did not, narrowing or reversing the robot's disadvantage"
- **Abstract says:** "we identify embarrassment associated with the service context as an important boundary condition. Further, we find that perceived creepiness of human (but not humanoid robot) frontline employees is contingent on service context."
- **Problem:** The abstract says human creepiness is contingent on context but does not state that it rose in embarrassing contexts, nor that the robot's disadvantage narrowed or reversed.
- **Suggested fix:** "State that human (but not robot) creepiness varied with service context and that embarrassment was an important boundary condition, flagging the specific pattern as not detailed in the abstract."

### Study 8: Gluten-free shoppers aren't asking for more choice — they want bread that tastes good and is safe
**Work ID:** W7222470326 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline overstates the variety finding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Gluten-free shoppers aren't asking for more choice — they want bread that tastes good and is safe"
- **Abstract says:** "product quality has the strongest association with consumer satisfaction, followed by service quality and product variety. ... Consumers report dissatisfaction with the limited availability of key product categories such as bread, pastry and ready-to-eat meals."
- **Problem:** Variety was still a positive correlate of satisfaction, just the weakest of three, and respondents explicitly complained about limited availability — so "aren't asking for more choice" overstates the result.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reframe as "quality and safety matter more than breadth of range — but the bread and ready-meal shelves still fall short.""

**Issue B. Added gloss on "safety"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Safety (freedom from cross-contamination) and taste were the most valued product attributes"
- **Abstract says:** "Safety and taste emerge as the most valued product attributes."
- **Problem:** The abstract does not define safety as freedom from cross-contamination; the parenthetical is the digest's interpretation.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop the parenthetical or mark it as an interpretation."

### Study 9: How close the disaster feels decides whether tourists boycott a destination
**Work ID:** W7221524554 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Mediation overread** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the damage operates through felt unfairness rather than the failure itself"
- **Abstract says:** "perceived relative deprivation and trust in destinations sequentially mediated the impact of the scopes of service failure crises on tourism boycott"
- **Problem:** Serial mediation means the failure's effect travels through deprivation and trust; it does not show the failure itself is not the source of the damage.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say the effect of crisis scope travels through perceived relative deprivation and then eroded trust."

**Issue B. Theoretical framing incomplete** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Two experiments grounded in construal level theory"
- **Abstract says:** "Grounded in self-bias theory and construal level theory"
- **Problem:** One of the two stated theoretical foundations is omitted.
- **Suggested fix:** "Add self-bias theory alongside construal level theory."

### Study 10: For small-business clients, getting the order right beats having the slickest logistics tech
**Work ID:** W7215042510 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 11: Corner shops can win the speed game without any of the quick-commerce infrastructure
**Work ID:** W7215042272 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Unsupported specification of digital service quality** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "basic digital service quality (chat ordering and similar lightweight tools)"
- **Abstract says:** "showing how social proximity, lightweight digital interaction and delivery responsiveness can create competitive advantage in informal retail environments"
- **Problem:** The abstract refers only to "lightweight digital interaction"; it never specifies chat/messaging ordering as the operationalization of digital service quality.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "lightweight digital interaction" or mark chat ordering as an illustrative example not specified in the abstract."

**Issue B. Perceived vs. actual speed comparison** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "and the feeling of speed, more than literal delivery minutes, is what drives where we buy"
- **Abstract says:** "It distinguishes perceived immediacy from infrastructural scale and positions perceived nanostore competitiveness as a consumer-level evaluative mechanism."
- **Problem:** The study measured perceptions only; it did not compare perceived immediacy against actual delivery times, so a "more than literal delivery minutes" ranking is not established.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to "perceived immediacy, rather than logistics scale, is what the study links to purchase intention.""

### Study 12: When your hashtag gets hijacked, the angriest posts aren't the ones that spread
**Work ID:** W7206212528 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Hedge dropped on diffusion finding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the most negative messages did not spread further once a conversation was already negatively skewed"
- **Abstract says:** "the findings suggest that negative messages do not necessarily achieve greater diffusion within negatively skewed bashtag conversations"
- **Problem:** The abstract says negativity does not *necessarily* produce greater diffusion; the digest converts a hedged null-ish result into a flat statement that the harshest posts did not spread.
- **Suggested fix:** "Add the hedge: "the most negative messages did not necessarily spread further...""

**Issue B. "Single market context" caveat** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Two brands and two campaigns in a single market context"
- **Abstract says:** "This study analyzed 14,511 posts related to McDonald's and Walkers Crisps"
- **Problem:** The abstract does not specify a market, and the two brands are associated with different markets (US and UK), so describing the evidence as coming from a single market is unverifiable from the abstract and probably inaccurate.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to "two brands and two campaigns only; market context not specified in the abstract.""

### Study 13: What a million words of app-store griping reveals about fintech users' well-being
**Work ID:** W7222527276 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Corpus size in headline** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "What a million words of app-store griping reveals about fintech users' well-being"
- **Abstract says:** "We applied a sequential mixed-methods design guided by Computational User Feedback Analytics (CUFA) to Arabic and English reviews collected from the Google Play Store and Apple App Store."
- **Problem:** The abstract gives no review or word count, so "a million words" is an invented figure. The abstract also frames the reviews as everyday experience data, not specifically complaints ("griping").
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop the quantity, e.g. "What unsolicited app-store reviews reveal about fintech users' well-being.""

### Study 14: Rude customers make staff less caring — and the boss's favorites take it hardest
**Work ID:** W7220440663 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Spillover to subsequent customers** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "it quietly drains the employee's capacity to be kind to the next several customers in line"
- **Abstract says:** "Results indicated a significant negative indirect effect of customer incivility on compassionate service behavior through workplace uncertainty."
- **Problem:** The study measured self-reported compassionate service behavior across survey waves, not carry-over to specific subsequent customers, so the "next several customers in line" framing implies a granularity the data don't have.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to "is linked to employees reporting less compassionate behavior toward customers generally.""

### Study 15: Speed is a luxury killer: what 1.2 million Google reviews say about AI in high-end service
**Work ID:** W7220919414 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 16: Foreign-branded universities: students say the country ties matter more than the price
**Work ID:** W7221546035 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 17: Faith-aligned features won't save a glitchy app: evidence from Islamic mobile banking reviews
**Work ID:** W7216405737 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Complaint clustering presented as a finding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "complaints clustered around system updates, verification processes, core banking functionality and stability — basic reliability, not religious compliance"
- **Abstract says:** "Islamic banks should prioritize improvements in system updates, verification processes, financial and banking functionalities, and overall system stability. Deficiencies in these fundamental service attributes generate negative emotional responses"
- **Problem:** The abstract presents these four areas as priority improvement recommendations tied to negative emotional responses, not as a measured distribution showing complaints concentrated there. The implied contrast with religious compliance is also the digest's addition — the abstract reports adherence to Islamic attributes as a significant positive contributor to satisfaction.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to "the authors direct managers to system updates, verification, core banking functionality and stability, where deficiencies triggered negative emotional responses" and drop the implied either/or with Islamic attributes."

## Issue Summary

| Study # | Headline | Verdict | Notes |
|---------|----------|---------|-------|
| 1 | What 141,000 Consumer Complaints Reveal About Why Disputes Escalate in Poorer Neighborhoods | ⚠️ Minor issues | Study facts and the direction of all reported associations match the abstract; the "Why it matters" line implies a comparison with failure severity that the abstract never tests. |
| 2 | When Rival Airlines Share the Same Big Investors, Service Gets Worse and Fares Go Up | ✅ Accurate | Dataset (U.S. airlines, 1995-2025), direction of effects and both moderators (attenuated by customer-asset value, amplified for multi-market rivals) all match; caveats correctly flag the observational panel design. |
| 3 | Fixing a Bad Meal? Compensate the Friend Too — but Only in the Right Dose | ⚠️ Minor issues | Three experiments, the companion-presence effect, the tier x compensation-amount interaction and both mechanisms are reported correctly; only the consumption setting is embellished beyond the abstract. |
| 4 | Asking Service Staff to Sell: Whether It Energizes or Burns Them Out Depends on the Climate You Set | ✅ Accurate | Dual-path mechanism (promotion/challenge/engagement vs prevention/hindrance/burnout), the work-meaningfulness moderator and the division of labour between field study and complementary experiment are all represented correctly. |
| 5 | Devout Customers Reported More Willingness to Be Rude to Staff — Unless Karma Was on Their Minds | ⚠️ Minor issues | Samples (202/279/297), mediator and karma boundary condition all match; one phrase implies a comparison of effect size across studies that the abstract does not make. |
| 6 | Not all workplace stress is bad: the kind that makes staff steal — and the kind that stops them | ⚠️ Minor issues | 708 employees across three studies, the challenge/hindrance split, the self-efficacy mechanism and the two moderators are reported correctly; the direction attributed to the peer-led development moderator is not stated in the abstract. |
| 7 | Customers find humanoid service robots creepy — except when the service is embarrassing | ⚠️ Minor issues | Two studies, the warmth/creepiness/comfort/intentions chain and the embarrassment boundary condition match; the described direction and magnitude of the human-employee creepiness shift goes beyond the abstract. |
| 8 | Gluten-free shoppers aren't asking for more choice — they want bread that tastes good and is safe | ⚠️ Minor issues | N=444, method and the ranking of satisfaction drivers match; the headline's "aren't asking for more choice" sits awkwardly against the abstract's finding of dissatisfaction with limited availability, and the cross-contamination gloss is added. |
| 9 | How close the disaster feels decides whether tourists boycott a destination | ⚠️ Minor issues | Two experiments, the personal > communal > external hierarchy, the serial mediation and the power-distance moderator are all accurate; the "Why it matters" line overstates what mediation shows and the digest drops self-bias theory. |
| 10 | For small-business clients, getting the order right beats having the slickest logistics tech | ✅ Accurate | N=236 Thai SMEs, SEM, direct plus satisfaction-mediated effects on repurchase intention, and the primacy of order accuracy and personnel contact over technology and corporate image all match; Harman's single-factor test correctly noted in caveats. |
| 11 | Corner shops can win the speed game without any of the quick-commerce infrastructure | ⚠️ Minor issues | Design, sample and mediation pattern all match the abstract; two small embellishments (the "chat ordering" example and the "feeling of speed beats delivery minutes" claim) go slightly past what the abstract states. |
| 12 | When your hashtag gets hijacked, the angriest posts aren't the ones that spread | ⚠️ Minor issues | Sample sizes, methods and the counter-negativity finding match; the digest states the diffusion result slightly more firmly than the abstract's hedged wording, and the "single market context" caveat is questionable for a US/UK brand pair. |
| 13 | What a million words of app-store griping reveals about fintech users' well-being | ⚠️ Minor issues | Method pipeline, the four experiential factors and the direction of each effect all match; only the headline's "million words" figure is unsupported. |
| 14 | Rude customers make staff less caring — and the boss's favorites take it hardest | ⚠️ Minor issues | Design (four-wave Prolific survey, N=316, US), the uncertainty mediator and the exacerbating high-LMX moderation are all reported correctly, and the correlational caveat is present; only the consumer-facing "next several customers" line overreaches. |
| 15 | Speed is a luxury killer: what 1.2 million Google reviews say about AI in high-end service | ✅ Accurate | Corpus size, dual-coding design, the five archetypes and the LLM's failure to detect Kairos deficits all match the abstract, and the caveats already flag that only 2,000 reviews were human-coded and that the archetypes are interpretive. |
| 16 | Foreign-branded universities: students say the country ties matter more than the price | ✅ Accurate | Sample (N=1,199), host and affiliate countries, the "at least 70 per cent" figure and country brand authenticity outranking financial factors are all reproduced correctly, and the descriptive, non-causal nature is flagged. |
| 17 | Faith-aligned features won't save a glitchy app: evidence from Islamic mobile banking reviews | ⚠️ Minor issues | Method (lexicon-based text mining plus panel regression, Indonesia) and the satisfaction drivers match; the claim that complaints "clustered" around four specific areas restates a managerial recommendation as a frequency finding. |

**Total issues:** 16 (16 Minor, 0 Moderate, 0 Major)
**Entries requiring revision:** 12
**Entries cleared:** 5
